title: Cross-Chain Bridges Guide: Moving Assets Across Blockchains
subtitle: Master cross-chain transfers - bridge types, security, aggregators, and best practices

intro.title: Understanding Bridges
intro.content:
Blockchain bridges are protocols that enable the transfer of assets and data between different blockchain networks. As the crypto ecosystem has expanded to dozens of chains, bridges have become essential infrastructure for moving value across this fragmented landscape.

Bridges solve a fundamental problem: blockchains are isolated by design. Bitcoin cannot natively communicate with Ethereum, and Ethereum cannot directly interact with Solana. Bridges create these connections, enabling true multi-chain experiences.

This guide covers everything from basic bridging concepts to advanced security considerations and optimization strategies.

why_bridges.title: Why Bridges Matter
why_bridges.content: Understanding why bridges are necessary helps you make better decisions about when and how to use them.

multi_chain_world.title: The Multi-Chain Reality
multi_chain_world.content:
The blockchain ecosystem has evolved from Ethereum dominance to a multi-chain world:

  • Layer 2s: Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, zkSync offer cheaper transactions
  • Alt L1s: Solana, Avalanche, BSC serve different use cases
  • App-specific chains: dYdX, Osmosis built for specific applications

Each chain has unique advantages - lower fees, faster transactions, specific DeFi protocols, or NFT communities. Bridges let you access all of them.

use_cases.title: Common Bridging Use Cases
use_cases.content:
DeFi opportunities: Access yield farms, lending protocols, or DEXs on other chains where returns may be higher or fees lower.

NFT access: Buy NFTs on Solana or trade on Blur (Ethereum) by bridging between chains.

Gas optimization: Move to L2s for 10-100x cheaper transactions while maintaining Ethereum security.

Airdrops: Many protocols require activity on multiple chains for eligibility.

Portfolio diversification: Spread risk across different chains and ecosystems.

bridge_types.title: Types of Bridges
bridge_types.content: Different bridge designs offer different tradeoffs between speed, cost, security, and decentralization.

lock_mint.title: Lock & Mint Bridges
lock_mint.content:
The most common bridge design. Assets are locked on the source chain, and wrapped tokens are minted on the destination.

How it works:

  1. You deposit ETH into a bridge contract on Ethereum
  2. The bridge verifies your deposit
  3. Wrapped ETH (wETH) is minted on the destination chain
  4. To return, wrapped tokens are burned and original assets unlocked

Pros: Simple to understand, widely supported

Cons: Creates wrapped assets (not native), centralization risks if bridge is compromised

burn_mint.title: Burn & Mint (Native) Bridges
burn_mint.content:
Some assets can be natively bridged without wrapping, maintaining full fungibility.

Circle CCTP enables native USDC transfers:

  • USDC is burned on the source chain
  • Native USDC is minted on the destination
  • No wrapped tokens - same USDC everywhere

This is the gold standard for bridging - you receive the exact same asset, not a wrapped version.

Advantage: Native assets have better liquidity and no smart contract risk from wrapping.

liquidity_network.title: Liquidity Network Bridges
liquidity_network.content:
Instead of minting new tokens, liquidity network bridges swap with existing assets on the destination chain.

How it works:

  1. You deposit ETH on Arbitrum
  2. Liquidity providers who hold ETH on Ethereum fulfill your transfer
  3. You receive native ETH (not wrapped) on Ethereum

Examples:

  • Across: Uses an optimistic oracle for fast, cheap transfers
  • Stargate: Unified liquidity pools across chains
  • Hop: AMM-based bridging with Bonder network

Advantages: Fast (minutes vs hours), native assets, competitive rates

canonical_bridges.title: Canonical (Official) Bridges
canonical_bridges.content:
Every L2 has an official bridge operated by the chain itself.

Characteristics:

  • Maximum security - secured by the L2's own validators
  • Usually slower (7 days for Optimistic Rollups to withdraw)
  • No additional trust assumptions beyond the L2 itself

When to use:

  • Large amounts where security is paramount
  • Initial deposits to L2s
  • When you're not in a hurry

Third-party bridges are faster but add additional trust assumptions.

getting_started.title: Your First Bridge Transfer
getting_started.content: Ready to bridge? Here's how to get started safely and efficiently.

first_bridge.title: Step-by-Step Guide
first_bridge.content:
Before bridging:

  • Have native gas tokens on the destination chain (or use gas refuel)
  • Verify you're on the official bridge URL
  • Start with a small test amount

Process:

  1. Connect your wallet to the bridge
  2. Select source and destination chains
  3. Choose the token and amount to bridge
  4. Review fees and expected time
  5. Approve token spending (if first time)
  6. Confirm the bridge transaction
  7. Wait for confirmation on both chains

Recommended for beginners: Across Protocol offers fast, reliable transfers with a simple interface.

choosing_bridge.title: How to Choose a Bridge
choosing_bridge.content:
Factors to consider:

  • Speed: Ranges from minutes (liquidity bridges) to 7 days (canonical)
  • Cost: Bridge fees + gas on both chains
  • Security: Track record, audit history, TVL
  • Supported assets: Not all bridges support all tokens
  • Native vs wrapped: Do you get the real asset?

Pro tip: Use bridge aggregators like LI.FI or Jumper to compare options automatically. They route through the best bridge for your specific transfer.

gas_optimization.title: Gas Optimization & Refueling
gas_optimization.content:
The gas problem: When you bridge to a new chain, you need native tokens for gas. But how do you pay for transactions if you have no gas tokens?

Solutions:

  • Gas refuel: Services like Bungee let you swap a small amount for destination gas
  • Faucets: Some testnets and new chains offer free gas
  • CEX withdrawal: Withdraw directly to L2 from exchanges

Cost tips:

  • Bridge during low gas periods (weekends, off-peak hours)
  • Batch multiple transfers into one
  • Use L2s for intermediate hops when possible

aggregators.title: Bridge Aggregators
aggregators.content: Bridge aggregators compare multiple bridges and routes to find the best option for your transfer.

why_aggregators.title: Why Use Aggregators?
why_aggregators.content:
With dozens of bridges available, manually comparing them is impractical.

Aggregators provide:

  • Automatic route optimization
  • Fee comparison across bridges
  • Speed estimates
  • Single interface for all bridges
  • Sometimes better rates through split routing

Think of them like flight comparison sites - they search all options so you don't have to.

top_aggregators.title: Top Aggregators
top_aggregators.content:
LI.FI is the most comprehensive:

  • Integrates 15+ bridges and 20+ DEXs
  • Cross-chain swaps (bridge + swap in one tx)
  • SDK for developers

Jumper (powered by LI.FI):

  • User-friendly interface
  • Gas refuel built-in
  • Transaction tracking

Socket (Bungee):

  • Focus on gas efficiency
  • Refuel feature for getting gas on new chains
  • Developer-friendly APIs

security.title: Bridge Security
security.content: Bridges are high-value targets and have suffered some of crypto's largest hacks. Understanding risks is essential.

bridge_risks.title: Understanding Bridge Risks
bridge_risks.content:
Why bridges are risky:

  • Large TVL: Billions locked makes them attractive targets
  • Complexity: Multi-chain code is harder to secure
  • Trust assumptions: Most require trusting validators or oracles
  • Smart contract risk: Bugs can drain entire bridge

Types of vulnerabilities:

  • Validator key compromise
  • Smart contract exploits
  • Oracle manipulation
  • Signature verification bugs

Over $2 billion has been stolen from bridges since 2021.

major_hacks.title: Notable Bridge Hacks
major_hacks.content: Learning from past incidents helps understand what to look for.

case_ronin.title: Ronin Bridge Hack ($625M)
case_ronin.description: In March 2022, hackers compromised 5 of 9 validator keys securing the Ronin Bridge (Axie Infinity). The attackers were able to forge withdrawals, draining 173,600 ETH and 25.5M USDC. The hack went unnoticed for 6 days. This highlighted the risks of centralized validator sets.

case_wormhole.title: Wormhole Hack ($320M)
case_wormhole.description: In February 2022, a signature verification bug allowed an attacker to mint 120,000 wETH on Solana without depositing on Ethereum. The vulnerability was in the smart contract code that verified guardian signatures. Jump Crypto later covered the losses.

best_practices.title: Security Best Practices
best_practices.content:
Before bridging:

  • Verify the URL carefully - bookmark official sites
  • Check the bridge's audit history and TVL
  • Start with small amounts to test
  • Research recent security incidents

Amount considerations:

  • For large amounts, consider using canonical bridges despite delays
  • Split large transfers across multiple bridges
  • Don't leave assets sitting in bridge contracts

Ongoing vigilance:

  • Follow bridge projects on social media for security updates
  • Monitor your transactions until confirmed on destination
  • Be cautious with new or unaudited bridges

advanced.title: Advanced Topics
advanced.content: Beyond simple asset transfers, bridges enable sophisticated cross-chain applications.

messaging_protocols.title: Cross-Chain Messaging
messaging_protocols.content:
Messaging protocols go beyond asset transfers to enable cross-chain contract calls.

LayerZero:

  • Omnichain messaging with configurable security
  • Powers Stargate and many omnichain tokens
  • Modular security model

Wormhole:

  • Guardian network verifies messages
  • Supports 20+ chains including Solana
  • General message passing

Hyperlane:

  • Permissionless deployment
  • Modular security options
  • Focus on developer experience

These protocols enable true cross-chain dApps - apps that can call contracts on other chains.

intent_based.title: Intent-Based Bridging
intent_based.content:
The newest generation of bridges uses "intents" - you specify what you want, and solvers compete to fulfill it.

How it works:

  1. You sign an intent: "I want 1 ETH on Arbitrum"
  2. Solvers compete to fulfill your intent
  3. Winner fronts the capital and is reimbursed later
  4. You receive funds in seconds

Advantages:

  • Faster execution (solvers have capital ready)
  • Better prices (competition between solvers)
  • Improved UX (simpler transactions)

Across Protocol pioneered this approach and remains the leader in intent-based bridging.

nft_bridging.title: NFT Bridging
nft_bridging.content:
Moving NFTs between chains is more complex than fungible tokens.

Challenges:

  • NFT metadata and images may need migration
  • Collection contracts must exist on destination
  • Provenance and history don't automatically transfer

Options:

  • Portal Bridge: Wormhole-based NFT transfers
  • LayerZero ONFTs: Omnichain NFT standard
  • Native NFT bridges: Some L2s have official NFT bridges

Caution: NFT bridging is less mature than token bridging. Always verify the bridged NFT is recognized on the destination chain's marketplaces.

canonical_bridge.definition: The official bridge operated by a blockchain network. These bridges have the highest security guarantees but often longer withdrawal times (7 days for Optimistic Rollups).

wrapped_token.definition: A token that represents another asset on a different chain. For example, wETH on Polygon represents ETH locked on Ethereum. Wrapped tokens add smart contract risk.

native_token.definition: The original, unwrapped version of a token on its home chain. Native tokens have better liquidity and no wrapping-related risks.

liquidity_pool.definition: Funds locked in smart contracts that enable instant bridging without waiting for cross-chain messages. LPs earn fees from bridge users.

finality.definition: The point at which a transaction is irreversible. Different chains have different finality times, affecting how quickly bridges can confirm transfers.

relayer.definition: A third party that submits transactions on behalf of users. Relayers often advance funds for faster bridging and are reimbursed later.

slippage.definition: The difference between expected and actual bridge output, often due to price movements during transfer or liquidity constraints.

gas_refuel.definition: A service that provides native gas tokens on the destination chain, solving the problem of having no gas to execute transactions after bridging.

omnichain.definition: A design philosophy where applications and tokens can operate across all chains seamlessly, often powered by messaging protocols like LayerZero.

intent.definition: A signed message expressing what the user wants (e.g., 'I want 1 ETH on Arbitrum'). Solvers compete to fulfill intents, resulting in better UX and prices.
